blocks.text: The rain hasn’t stopped since eight, and Blackwood Lane wears it like a held breath. Number 17 glows against the dark — every window lit, the porch light buzzing, a black-and-white parked crooked at the curb with its light bar still turning, painting the wet hedges red and blue.
You duck under the crime-scene tape and climb the steps. A uniformed officer waits under the porch overhang, collar up, notebook already damp at the edges. She extends a hand.
Detective. Dana Reyes — first on scene. The victim’s Daniel Whitmore, fifty-two, in the study. His wife’s inside. She says she shot him — says it was self-defense, an argument that went wrong.
I took wide shots of the house and the study before the rain got worse. They’re yours. The wife’s in the living room, the daughter’s upstairs. Nobody’s touched the study since I taped it.

Through the front door you can see the living room — a woman sitting very still on the edge of a sofa, hands folded, not crying. Beyond, a hallway leads toward the study. The whole house smells of rain and woodsmoke, with something metallic underneath it.
Case opened: The House at Blackwood Lane. Work the scene before you begin interviews.

choices.label: Examine the grounds
choices.sub: Walk the perimeter before going in.

blocks.text: The back walk is mud — the rain has turned the garden into something that keeps score. Your flashlight finds them halfway to the rear door: men’s prints, size eleven or so, pressed deep, heading toward the house.

You follow them back the other way. They come from the side gate, not the street. And here’s the thing worth writing down: they don’t go back. Whoever walked in through the mud never walked out the way he came — at least, not by the front.
The rear of the house is dark. A ground-floor window — the study, by the layout — shows a smear at latch height, though you’ll want to look closer at that from the inside.
Find something, Detective?
You don’t answer yet. You photograph the prints and mark their line with little flags. The rain is already softening the edges, washing the night’s arithmetic away.

The side gate hangs ajar, its latch rusted open. Beyond it, the lane is empty, rain drumming on parked cars. Whoever came through here knew the house — knew the gate, knew the dark stretch of the walk, knew which window belonged to the study.

choices.label: Head back inside
choices.sub: The rain is washing the prints away.

blocks.text: The living room is too warm and too quiet. Eleanor Whitmore sits on the edge of the sofa in a dark dress, hands folded in her lap, a blanket someone — Reyes, probably — draped over her shoulders. She looks up when you enter. Her eyes are dry. That isn’t guilt; you’ve seen enough grief to know it doesn’t always leak.

Above the mantel hangs the family photograph: the three Whitmores on this very porch, three summers ago, smiling into the sun. Daniel’s arm around his daughter. His smile doesn’t reach his eyes. You know that look. You’ve worn it at fundraisers.
Detective. Whatever you need — I’ll tell you everything. I just… I need a moment before the questions.
You nod and take the photograph down carefully, bag it. A young woman — the daughter, Claire — hovers in the hallway beyond, half in shadow, watching. She disappears when your eyes find her.

The study smells of leather, gun oil, and rain coming through a window someone left cracked. Daniel Whitmore lies on the rug under a sheet, and the room has arranged itself around him like a held note — desk, lamp still burning, a pistol resting on the blotter where no pistol should rest.

The sheet covers him completely; only the shape of a man remains, and a dark stain the rug has drunk at its edge. You stand in the doorway a moment and let the room talk. The desk drawers hang open. The window latch glints. Daniel’s phone lies face-down beside a cold cup of coffee. Everything in here is a question wearing a room’s clothes.
Take your time, Detective. Nobody’s touching anything until you say so.
The rain ticks against the glass. Somewhere upstairs, a floorboard complains — the daughter, probably, or the house settling around what’s happened in it.
Work the scene. When you’ve looked at the body and the gun, Reyes will let you begin the interviews.

choices.label: Examine the firearm
choices.sub: A pistol lies on the desk.

choices.label: Study the blood pattern
choices.sub: The rug tells its own story.

choices.label: Begin the interviews
choices.sub: Talk to the people in this house.
choices.ifHint: Not yet, Detective — you haven’t looked at the body or the gun.

blocks.text: You kneel beside the sheet and fold it back with gloved hands, only as far as you need. Daniel Whitmore, fifty-two. One wound, center chest. You don’t look long — the dead deserve efficiency — but you look carefully.

It’s the blood that argues with the room. The pooling, the lividity settling in his back and shoulders — it doesn’t match how he’s lying. He was moved, thirty minutes or so after death, dragged a short distance across the rug and left to present a tidier scene than the one he died in.
Eleanor’s account — a shot fired in panic, a body fallen where it fell — doesn’t explain this. Someone rearranged the truth after the trigger was pulled.
Dispatch update received.

Reyes watches from the doorway, quiet for once. “Thirty minutes, give or take,” she murmurs, reading your face. You nod. Thirty minutes after death, someone stood where you’re standing and moved a dead man like furniture.
You fold the sheet back into place with the same care you took removing it. The dead can’t be helped, but they can be respected. The living, though — the living still have questions to answer.

The pistol sits on the blotter like an exhibit that posed itself. Daniel Whitmore’s registered weapon — Reyes already ran the serial. You lift it with a pen through the trigger guard and turn it under the lamp.

It’s clean. Not “wiped down” clean — forensically clean. No prints at all. Not Daniel’s. Not Eleanor’s, though she says she fired it. Someone took a cloth to this gun after the shooting and erased everyone who ever touched it.
People wipe guns for one reason: to decide what the gun is allowed to say. Whoever cleaned this one was thinking clearly, and thinking about the future.

You turn the pistol over once more, checking the grip, the slide, the muzzle. Nothing. A gun this clean has a history it’s been forbidden to tell — and the man who forbade it stood in this room tonight, thinking about tomorrow.
Somebody wanted this gun to be a mystery.
You don’t correct her. Somebody wanted this gun to be innocent.

The desk is a battlefield of paper. Daniel’s laptop sits open, its screen dark — encrypted, but the file index shows a massacre of deletions timestamped 9:14 PM. Daniel died around 8:47. Somebody used this machine after he was dead, and they were in a hurry.

In the top drawer, under a stack of charity gala programs, a handwritten note in a hurried hand: “If anything happens — ask M.V. Everything is in the second drawer. — D.” M.V. You already know a Marcus Vale exists in Daniel’s orbit. Now you know Daniel was afraid enough to write it down.

The second drawer sticks. When you press the side panel, the wood gives a quarter inch — a hidden compartment, shallow, dust-lined. Something sat in there a long time. Your thumbnail finds the edge of the panel.

You photograph the note, the laptop, the drawer’s false panel, each in turn. Methodical. The room rewards patience — it hid a compartment for years, and it will hide its other secrets just as long if you rush.
That second drawer — you want me to log it as a concealment?
Log everything. Especially the things that were meant to stay hidden.

choices.label: Pry open the loose second drawer
choices.sub: The panel is begging to come off.

do.text: Hidden compartment: a page of coded payments — “ORPHEUS — Q3 disbursements.”

choices.label: Step back
choices.sub: The desk has told you enough.

blocks.text: The study window is latched — but the latch is wrong. Mud on the sill, mud smeared across the latch itself, and a long smear down the outside frame where a shoe slid. Someone climbed out of this window recently, in a hurry, in the rain.
You hold your flashlight to the mud and then think of the back walk. Same soil, same rain. Whoever left through this window walked in through the mud first.
The front door would have been simpler. You only leave through a window when you don’t want to be seen leaving — and only after doing something you don’t want found.
You sketch the smear in your notebook: latch, sill, outer frame. The pattern is unmistakable — a gloved hand on the latch, a shoulder against the frame, a shoe finding purchase and slipping.
Outside, the rain has already begun its own cleanup. By morning there’ll be nothing left out there. But in here — in here the window remembers.
So our visitor left through the window.
Our visitor didn’t want the front door to know he’d been here.
Daniel’s phone is face-down on the blotter, as if he’d set it aside mid-thought and never picked it up. You bag it, glove it, wake it with the department kit. Two things surface.
First: a week of texts from an unknown number, each one colder than the last. “You don’t get to walk away.” “We made you, Daniel.” “Thursday. Decide.” Daniel was being leaned on, and he knew it.
Second: the call log. At 9:02 PM — forty-four minutes after the shooting, twenty-nine minutes before Eleanor called 911 — Eleanor called Marcus Vale. She never mentioned that call to Reyes.
Your own phone buzzes in your pocket. Unknown number. You already know, the way you know rain, that this isn’t a coincidence.
You scroll the threats once more, memorizing the cadence. Whoever wrote them knew Daniel — knew what he’d built, and what walking away would cost. “Thursday. Decide.” Thursday was two days ago.

And then your own phone buzzes. You stare at the unknown number for a long moment before you understand: someone is watching this investigation in real time. Someone who knew the moment you touched Daniel’s phone.

message.text: Detective. Some stones are better left unturned.

response.text: Someone who liked Daniel better alive. Leave Blackwood.

blocks.text: You step back and read the rug the way you’d read a map. The cast-off arcs, the drag marks running two feet across the weave — the body was pulled after the bleeding slowed. Not carried. Dragged, by someone who didn’t want to lift him.
Thirty minutes after death, give or take. Someone came back to the body — or arrived after — and went through him. The pockets of Daniel’s jacket hang wrong, turned half inside-out.
Eleanor says she fired in panic and called for help. Nothing about moving him. Nothing about going through his pockets. The rug says otherwise, and rugs don’t panic.

You crouch and trace the drag marks with your flashlight, not touching. Two feet. The rug fibers lie in combed lines, all pointing the same way — toward the desk, as if the body had been pulled closer to something, or away from it.
Searched, you think?
Searched. Pockets turned. Somebody wanted something Daniel was carrying — or wanted us to think they did.
Either way, Eleanor’s story has a hole in it now, two feet wide, shaped like a dragged man.

The living room has become an interview room with better furniture. Reyes has arranged it with a uniform’s efficiency: Eleanor on the sofa, Marcus Vale — arrived twenty minutes ago, coat still damp — in the armchair like he owns it, Claire hovering by the window, and Dr. Cole, summoned by phone, perched on the piano bench looking like he’d rather be anywhere else.
You take the chair facing them all. Four people, four versions of Daniel Whitmore. Somewhere under the floorboards of this house, the truth is keeping very still.
Detective. Tragic business. Whatever I can do to help — Daniel was like a brother to me.
Claire flinches at that. Eleanor doesn’t look at him at all. Interesting.
Rain needles the windows. The four of them avoid each other’s eyes with the discipline of people who have been avoiding them for years.
Eleanor’s holding. Vale’s performing. The girl’s terrified. Cole looks like he swallowed a secret. Your call, Detective — where do you want to start?
You set your notebook on your knee. One question at a time. That’s how houses like this give up their dead.

message.text: Interviews are set up in the living room whenever you’re ready.

blocks.text: Up close, Eleanor Whitmore’s composure has hairline cracks. Her hands tremble when she thinks you’re not looking. She folds them tighter.
We argued. About money — about the foundation, about… he’d changed, Detective. Tonight he was someone I didn’t recognize. He came at me — his hands —
She touches her throat without realizing. There are faint marks there — finger-shaped, already yellowing. You photograph them with your eyes.
The gun was in his drawer. I didn’t think. It just — went off. I held him while he… and then I couldn’t think at all.
It’s a clean account. Almost too clean. The 9:02 PM call sits between you like a third person in the room.
She twists a plain gold band around her finger, around and around. Twenty-six years of marriage, and tonight it ended in a drawer, a lunge, a shot.
I keep thinking if I’d just — if I hadn’t gone into the study. If I’d let him have his secrets. But I found the ledger, Detective. I found what he’d built. I couldn’t un-find it.
The ledger. She says it like a name she’s afraid to say twice.

choices.label: Ask her to walk you through the argument

do.text: Her account never wavers: the drawer, the lunge, the single shot. The throat marks back her up.

choices.label: Offer her a glass of water

do.text: Her hand steadies around the glass. “Thank you,” she says quietly. Something in her unclenches.
She breaks. “I called Marcus. I panicked — Daniel was dead and I didn’t know what to do. He said he’d handle it.”

choices.label: Leave her to her thoughts
choices.sub: You’ll come back if you need to.

blocks.text: Marcus Vale is fifty-five and wears it like tailoring. Silver hair, easy smile, eyes that do arithmetic while he talks. He crossed the room to shake your hand when you entered, as if this were his house and you his guest.
Daniel and I built Whitmore Logistics together — twenty years. And the foundation, of course. Ask anyone in Blackwood what Daniel meant to this town.
Where was I tonight? Home. Alone. A terrible thing, to hear it from a police officer’s mouth. Eleanor must be destroyed.
He says all of it smoothly. Too smoothly — the account of a man who rehearsed in the car. You notice mud on the welt of his left shoe, and he notices you noticing.
He leans back, perfectly at ease, and you understand: this is a man who has been interviewed before. By better people than you, probably. In rooms with worse lighting.
Daniel was a visionary. The foundation, the jobs, the giving — Blackwood doesn’t know what it lost. I intend to make sure his work continues.
“His work.” The phrase hangs there, and you both know it doesn’t mean the charity galas.

choices.label: Ask about his partnership with Daniel
choices.sub: Twenty years is a long time.

do.text: “Twenty years,” he says, spreading his hands. “Brothers, really.” The word sits oddly in his mouth.

choices.label: Press him on where he was tonight

do.text: “Home. Alone.” He smiles. “Check if you like. There’s no one to ask.”
The charm drops like a curtain. “I tidied up,” he says flatly. “The gun, the laptop — Daniel was dead when I arrived. You can’t prove otherwise.”

blocks.text: Claire Whitmore is twenty-four and looks sixteen tonight, wrapped in a cardigan, arms crossed tight. She keeps glancing at the hallway, as if the house itself might overhear.
I heard them fighting. Mom was crying — she never cries. Then the… the noise. I stayed in my room. I should have gone down. I should have —
She stops, breathing hard. You wait. Waiting is half the job.
Mr. Vale scares me. He’s always been… around. Watching. Mom says he’s family. He isn’t family.
She’s holding something back. Fear does that — locks the jaw around the one thing that matters.
She picks at a loose thread on her cardigan. The rain has eased, and through the window you can see the dark rectangle of Blackwood Lane, wet and empty.
Dad and Mr. Vale had a fight last month. Screaming, in the study. Dad said — he said “you don’t own me.” I’d never heard him talk like that. Not to anyone.
She looks up at you, suddenly fierce through the fear. “Whatever he did that night — Mr. Vale did something. I know it.”

choices.label: Ask what she heard that night

do.text: “The argument, then the shot. Then — later — a car. I didn’t see whose.” Her eyes flick toward the window.
“You’re safe here,” you tell her. “Nothing leaves this room without your say.” She exhales, and nods — once.

choices.label: Ask if she saw anything outside
choices.sub: Her eyes keep going to the window.

do.text: She pulls out her phone with shaking hands. “I took this from my window. 9:15. That’s Mr. Vale’s car.”

blocks.text: Dr. Adrian Cole sits on the piano bench with a doctor’s upright spine and a witness’s unhappy eyes. Sixty-three, physician to the Whitmores for two decades, and everything about him says he’d rather be reading a chart than sitting in this room.
Daniel was my patient and my friend. If you’re asking whether he was well — he wasn’t sleeping. He asked me about sedatives. I told him to try counting sheep like the rest of us.
He said… he said his associates worried him. I told him business stress, take a holiday. I wish I’d listened harder.
He stops there, the way ethical men do — at the exact border of what they think they’re allowed to say.
Cole removes his glasses and polishes them, a stall you’ve seen a hundred times. Doctors hate testifying — it offends their sense of order. The body is supposed to stay on the table.
He asked about sedatives. “To sleep,” he said. But men like Daniel don’t lose sleep over insomnia, Detective. They lose it over arithmetic — over what they owe, and to whom.
He puts the glasses back on. The stall is over.

choices.label: Ask about Daniel’s state of mind

do.text: “Anxious. Guarded. A man waiting for a letter he didn’t want to open.” Cole folds his hands. “That’s a diagnosis of sorts.”

choices.label: Ask directly: was Daniel afraid of someone?

do.text: Cole hesitates — then nods. “He believed they’d kill him if he tried to leave. His words, Detective. Not mine.”

blocks.text: Back in the study, the rain has thinned to a whisper. The sheet, the lamp, the clean gun in its bag — the room has given you everything it’s going to give. Reyes waits in the hall with her notebook closed, which for Reyes is practically a salute.

You lay it out in your head one last time. Eleanor fired the shot — the throat marks, her account, the forensics all agree. But the wiped gun, the moved body, the window, the 9:02 call, the ledger page with its coded millions: someone came after, and cleaned, and stole.
Marcus Vale was in this house tonight. The question is what you can prove — and what proving it costs. Three paths. One phone call.
Review your evidence. This decision is final.
Whatever you’re going to do, Detective — the DA’s already calling. They want a name by morning.

A name by morning. You look at the board in your head once more: the gun, the ledger, the window, the call, the photograph, the doctor’s warning. Every path costs someone. The only question is who pays, and for what.

choices.label: Lay out the whole truth: Eleanor acted in self-defense; charge Marcus Vale with tampering and theft.
choices.sub: The ledger, the wiped gun, the window, the call — it’s all connected.
choices.ifHint: You don’t have enough to prove the full sequence yet.

choices.label: Arrest Marcus Vale for the murder of Daniel Whitmore.
choices.sub: He was here that night. The rest is noise.

blocks.text: You make the call. Justifiable self-defense. The paperwork practically writes itself — the throat marks, the consistent account, the forensics that back her.

Eleanor walks out of the living room into the rain without handcuffs. Claire holds her mother’s arm. Marcus Vale watches from the porch, expression unreadable, and then he’s gone into the dark like he was never there.
Case closed.
The drive back is quiet. Rain on the windshield, the town dark. You tell yourself the forensics backed her — the throat marks, the account, the single shot. It was self-defense. The file says so.
But files don’t mention wiped guns or ledger pages or mud on a window latch. You closed the case you could prove, and left the rest in the dark where it lives.
Some cases you solve. Some you survive. This one you’ll carry — the one where the truth was in your hands and you set it down, because proving it would have cost more than the file could hold.
You lay it out for Reyes, piece by piece — the wiped gun, the ledger page, the window, the 9:02 call. Her eyebrows climb with every item. By the end she’s on the radio.

They take Marcus Vale on the porch, in the rain, in front of the house he thought he’d cleaned. He doesn’t resist. “Daniel was dead when I arrived,” he says, as the cuffs close. “You can’t prove otherwise.”
Eleanor’s self-defense is ruled justified. The ledger goes to the state police in a sealed bag. And on the drive back, Reyes says what you’re both thinking: Blackwood was just one cell.

The station smells of coffee and wet wool. You write the report until your hand cramps: tampering, theft, obstruction. Every charge anchored to something you can hold — the cloth-wiped steel, the coded page, the mud, the call log.
It’s past two when you finish. Outside, the rain has finally stopped. Blackwood sleeps, unaware that tonight, for once, the truth got written down before the money could bury it.
You make the call. Marcus Vale, for the murder of Daniel Whitmore. The cuffs, the cameras, the DA’s press conference — it all moves so fast it feels like justice.
It isn’t. Forensics is patient and merciless: the ballistics, the residue patterns, the timeline — none of it puts the gun in Marcus’s hand. He never fired it. The charge collapses in eleven days.

The DA, embarrassed, reopens against Eleanor. She takes a manslaughter plea to make it stop. Marcus walks out of the courthouse into the sun, free, and the real story — the network, the cleanup, the ledger — is buried under your rush to judgment.
The press conference is a blur of flashes. The DA shakes your hand for the cameras. For eleven days, you’re the detective who caught a killer.

On the twelfth day, forensics calls. You listen to the ballistics report with the phone going cold against your ear, and understand — too late — the difference between being in the house and pulling the trigger.

EVIDENCE-001.name: Crime Scene Photographs
EVIDENCE-001.description: Wide shots of the house and study, taken by Officer Reyes before the rain worsened.
EVIDENCE-001.detail: Reyes photographed the exterior, the front hall, and the study before anything was moved. The study shots show the body where it was found, the pistol on the desk blotter, and the open drawers — a baseline the rest of the forensics will be measured against.

EVIDENCE-002.name: Muddy Footprints
EVIDENCE-002.description: Men’s size-11 prints in the mud along the back walk, heading toward the house — then none returning by the front.
EVIDENCE-002.detail: The prints enter via the side gate and stop at the rear of the house. No matching set leaves by the front walk. Whoever came in through the mud did not walk out the way visitors do.

EVIDENCE-003.name: Family Photograph
EVIDENCE-003.description: The Whitmores three years ago, smiling on this same porch. Daniel’s smile doesn’t reach his eyes.
EVIDENCE-003.detail: A framed porch portrait, three summers old: Daniel, Eleanor, and Claire. A happy family, or a family performing happiness. Daniel’s expression is the one men wear when the camera is the least of their problems.

EVIDENCE-004.name: Body Examination Notes
EVIDENCE-004.description: Single gunshot wound to the chest. Lividity and blood pooling inconsistent with the body’s position — it was moved ~30 minutes after death.
EVIDENCE-004.detail: One wound, center chest, fatal within minutes. But lividity has settled in the back and shoulders in a pattern that contradicts the position the body was found in. The body was moved roughly half an hour after death — dragged a short distance and repositioned.

EVIDENCE-005.name: Wiped Firearm
EVIDENCE-005.description: Daniel’s registered pistol. Forensically wiped clean — not a single print, not even Daniel’s or Eleanor’s. Someone cleaned it after the shooting.
EVIDENCE-005.detail: Serial matches Daniel Whitmore’s registration. The weapon is forensically sterile: no prints, no partials, no DNA — not even the owner’s or the woman who says she fired it. A panicked shooter does not stop to polish a gun. Someone thinking clearly did this, after the fact.

EVIDENCE-006.name: Daniel’s Laptop
EVIDENCE-006.description: Encrypted. File index shows large deletions made at 9:14 PM — after Daniel died. Someone used it after the murder.
EVIDENCE-006.detail: The drive is encrypted, but the file index survived: a mass deletion at 9:14 PM, nearly half an hour after Daniel’s death. Someone sat at this desk, after the shooting, and destroyed data in a hurry. The laptop itself was left behind — the thief ran out of time, or nerve.

EVIDENCE-007.name: Daniel’s Note
EVIDENCE-007.description: Handwritten, in the desk drawer: “If anything happens — ask M.V. Everything is in the second drawer. — D.”
EVIDENCE-007.detail: A hurried hand on foundation letterhead. Daniel Whitmore was afraid of something — or someone — and left instructions pointing at “M.V.” The second drawer he mentions sticks; its side panel gives a quarter inch under pressure.

EVIDENCE-008.name: Orpheus Ledger Page
EVIDENCE-008.description: Hidden compartment in the desk’s second drawer. A page of coded payments: “ORPHEUS — Q3 disbursements.” Proof of the network.
EVIDENCE-008.detail: A single folded page from a hidden compartment: columns of coded payments headed ORPHEUS — Q3 disbursements. Seven figures moving through shell entities tied to the Whitmore charitable foundation. This is not charity accounting. This is a private intelligence brokerage, and Daniel Whitmore was running it.

EVIDENCE-009.name: Muddy Window Smear
EVIDENCE-009.description: Mud smeared on the study window latch and sill — someone climbed out recently. Mud matches the back-walk soil.
EVIDENCE-009.detail: Mud on the latch, the sill, and a slide-smear down the outer frame: someone climbed out of the study window in the rain, recently. Soil composition matches the back walk — the same mud as the footprints. You only leave through a window when you don’t want to be seen leaving.

EVIDENCE-010.name: Blood Pattern Analysis
EVIDENCE-010.description: Cast-off and drag marks: the body was pulled about two feet across the rug after the bleeding slowed. Staged or searched post-mortem.
EVIDENCE-010.detail: Cast-off arcs and drag marks run two feet across the rug. The body was pulled — not carried — after the bleeding slowed, roughly thirty minutes post-mortem. The jacket pockets hang turned half inside-out: the body was searched, or the scene was staged to look searched.

EVIDENCE-011.name: Unknown Texts
EVIDENCE-011.description: Threatening texts on Daniel’s phone from an unknown number, received over the past week: “You don’t get to walk away.”
EVIDENCE-011.detail: A week of escalating messages from a blocked number: “You don’t get to walk away.” “We made you, Daniel.” “Thursday. Decide.” Daniel Whitmore was being leaned on by people he feared — and the pressure was building toward this week.

EVIDENCE-012.name: 9:02 PM Call Log
EVIDENCE-012.description: Eleanor called Marcus Vale at 9:02 PM — 29 minutes before she called 911.
EVIDENCE-012.detail: The call log is unambiguous: 9:02 PM, Eleanor Whitmore called Marcus Vale — forty-four minutes after the shooting, twenty-nine minutes before she dialed 911. She never mentioned this call to Officer Reyes. Whatever was said in those minutes, it happened before the police existed in her night.

EVIDENCE-013.name: Claire’s Photograph
EVIDENCE-013.description: Time-stamped 9:15 PM: a black sedan leaving Blackwood Lane. Registered to Marcus Vale. (Shared by Claire.)
EVIDENCE-013.detail: Taken from Claire Whitmore’s bedroom window at 9:15 PM: a black sedan pulling away down Blackwood Lane, plates readable. Registered to Vale Holdings — Marcus Vale’s company. Marcus Vale was here tonight, whatever his alibi says.

EVIDENCE-014.name: Dr. Cole’s Statement
EVIDENCE-014.description: Cole confirms Daniel feared “his associates” and believed they would kill him if he tried to leave.
EVIDENCE-014.detail: Dr. Adrian Cole, the family physician, states that Daniel Whitmore told him he feared “his associates” and believed they would kill him if he tried to walk away from their arrangement. Corroborates the threatening texts: Daniel was afraid of the people he worked with.

ENDING-A.title: The Official Story
ENDING-A.summary: Eleanor Whitmore’s self-defense claim is accepted and the case closes. Marcus Vale is never charged.
ENDING-A.epilogue: Three weeks later, a wire transfer marked ORPHEUS clears through a Blackwood account — seven figures, routed through three shells. The network survives. Somewhere, Marcus Vale pours a drink to Daniel’s memory, and the stones stay unturned.

ENDING-B.title: The Whole Truth
ENDING-B.summary: Marcus Vale is arrested for tampering, theft, and obstruction; Eleanor’s self-defense is ruled justified; the Orpheus ledger goes to the state police.
ENDING-B.epilogue: The ledger names eleven cities. Blackwood was just one cell. The state police open a task force, and your phone rings twice a week with questions you can’t answer yet. Marcus Vale hires four lawyers. Eleanor Whitmore plants roses over the place where the rug used to be. The truth, for once, got written down.

ENDING-C.title: The Wrong Man
ENDING-C.summary: Marcus Vale is arrested for murder — but forensics prove he never fired the gun. The case collapses; Eleanor takes a manslaughter plea; Marcus walks free.
ENDING-C.epilogue: The ledger never surfaces. ORPHEUS routes around Blackwood like water around a stone. Years later, you’ll still wake up thinking about the window latch, and the mud, and the difference between being in the house and pulling the trigger. Some stones, it turns out, bury you.

messages.text: Body confirmed at 17 Blackwood Lane. Victim: Daniel Whitmore. Spouse on scene.

response.text: En route. I’ll ping you when the preliminary lands.

database.name: Daniel Whitmore
database.summary: Blackwood philanthropist, 52. Owner of Whitmore Logistics. Registered owner of the pistol found in the study.
database.details: Founder of the Whitmore Charitable Foundation and CEO of Whitmore Logistics. No criminal record. Firearm registration on file matches the pistol recovered from the study (see EVIDENCE-005). Publicly a pillar of Blackwood; privately, the financial records suggest a second life his charity galas never mentioned.

database.name: Eleanor Whitmore
database.summary: Wife of the victim, 48. No criminal record.
database.details: Married to Daniel Whitmore for 26 years. No arrests, no warrants, no record of any kind. Listed as a trustee of the Whitmore Charitable Foundation. Currently at the scene, cooperating.

database.name: Marcus Vale
database.summary: Daniel Whitmore’s business partner, 55. Subject of a fraud investigation in 2019 — dropped for lack of evidence.
database.details: Co-founder of Whitmore Logistics and director of Vale Holdings. Investigated for corporate fraud in 2019; the case was dropped for lack of evidence. Known associate of Daniel Whitmore for twenty years. Alibi for tonight is unverified.

database.name: Claire Whitmore
database.summary: Daughter of Daniel and Eleanor Whitmore, 24. Graduate student.
database.details: Graduate student, lives at the family home. No record. Was home on the night of the shooting. Described by officers as frightened but cooperative.

database.name: Dr. Adrian Cole
database.summary: Family physician to the Whitmores, 63. Clean record.
database.details: Practicing physician, Blackwood General. Daniel Whitmore’s doctor for two decades. No malpractice history, no criminal record. Summoned to the scene to speak about Daniel’s state of mind in recent weeks.

database.name: ORPHEUS
database.summary: No official records. The ledger suggests a private intelligence network.
database.details: No incorporation papers, no tax filings, no official trace — and that is the point. The recovered ledger page describes coded quarterly disbursements moving through shell entities tied to the Whitmore foundation. Pattern is consistent with a private intelligence brokerage: buying and selling corporate secrets and leverage.

database.name: 17 Blackwood Lane
database.summary: Property record: single-family residence, owned by Daniel and Eleanor Whitmore since 2004.
database.details: Two-story colonial on a half-acre lot, purchased 2004. No liens. Alarm system registered but disarmed on the night in question. The study window — ground floor, rear — is noted in the original floor plan.

database.name: Black Sedan
database.details: Late-model black sedan. Plates trace to Vale Holdings — Marcus Vale’s company. Photographed leaving Blackwood Lane at 9:15 PM on the night of the shooting (see EVIDENCE-013).

theories.question: Was the body moved after death?

systemNotes.text: The body was moved after death — Eleanor’s account doesn’t explain this.
